name: Adam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We run six hundred sows at Thornbury, breeding pigs and taking them through to finished weight, and three hundred hectares of barley and wheat that mostly goes into our own feed. My day starts at six with a coffee and the shed dashboards on my phone: temperatures, water use, feed, any alarms overnight. Then I walk the farrowing house, that's where the sows have their piglets, because numbers tell you a lot, but you still need to smell the air.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My son Erik, who's thirty-two and runs the arable side. Four full-time stockmen, the best of them is Marek, who's been with me fourteen years. And a lad called Callum, eighteen, who I took on as an apprentice in September. My wife Kirsten is a receptionist at the dental surgery in town and keeps me honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making a system work. When the pigs grow well, the feed's from our own fields and the muck goes back on the land, it all fits together and there's real satisfaction in that. What wears me out is the pig price. It goes up and down like a fairground ride, and when it's down you can lose thirty pounds a pig.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I've got sensors that listen for coughing in the finishing sheds and flag it before you'd hear it yourself, and I ask an assistant to look over the feed costs and draft the paperwork. I was one of the first in the county with the cough monitors. Some of the older men thought I'd gone soft. Then their pigs got sick and mine didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, because it could do more. But a good tool is a good tool, and I'd keep using it. At the pig producers' meeting I'd tell the others to stop waiting and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes for me. The pig price and the feed price run my life, not AI. I'll keep using what works and ignore what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the new finishing shed, about three hundred thousand with a loan, which we've planned for two years. I'd keep Callum on and get him through his apprenticeship. And I'd try any new monitoring kit that comes along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit impatient. I'd like things to move faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three hundred thousand is a big loan with only a few months' savings. How do you think about that risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. We've got about four months' costs in the bank, which isn't much in a bad pig year. But the shed pays for itself in eight years if prices are average, and Erik will be here long after me. You can't farm scared. My father never borrowed a penny and the farm nearly died with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Callum.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's from the estate on the edge of town, his dad left when he was small. He turned up on time every day for a month and asked good questions, so I took him on. He's slow on the dashboards but brilliant with the sows, very calm. The college does the theory one day a week and Marek does the rest.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame AI isn't doing more, but a good tool is a good tool. I'd tell the pig producers to stop waiting and get on with it.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes, since the pig and feed prices run my life. I'll keep using what works and ignore what doesn't.
S0.do: Builds the planned three-hundred-thousand finishing shed with a loan and keeps Callum on through his apprenticeship. Tries new monitoring kit as it comes along.
S0.feel: Calm and a little impatient for faster change.
S0.quote: You can't farm scared. My father never borrowed a penny and the farm nearly died with him.
S0.fieldNote: He's comfortable with risk and debt in a way most farmers his age aren't, and he explains why with family history. His enthusiasm for technology sits alongside a strong sense of duty to train young people like Callum. Confident and plain-spoken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine, but firms not hiring beginners is a mistake they'll regret. Every business needs young people learning the trade, or you've got nobody in ten years. I'd say employers should step up with apprenticeships, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow suits me, I'll stay ahead of my neighbours. But I'd worry for lads like Callum. If the feed mills and the vets stop taking trainees, farms like mine are the only door left, and there aren't enough of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a second apprentice, probably from the same college, about twelve thousand a year after the grant. I'd talk to two other pig farmers about sharing apprentices, so the young ones see more than one farm. And I'd teach Callum the data side, slowly, because he'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but I'd feel a responsibility for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think it should be employers rather than the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we know what the job needs. A government scheme teaches you to fill in forms about pigs. A farmer teaches you to see a sow is about to farrow by the way she's nesting. I'm happy for the government to help pay, but the teaching should be on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in teaching Callum the data side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that he'll get too good and leave for a bigger company. That's fine. That's what an apprenticeship is for. If he goes on to run a big unit one day, I'll have done my bit.

S1.say: I'd say firms not hiring beginners will regret it, because every business needs young people learning the trade. Employers should step up with apprenticeships, not wait for the government.
S1.think: Privately slow suits me and keeps me ahead. I'd worry for lads like Callum if feed mills and vets stop taking trainees, since farms like mine would be the only door left.
S1.do: Takes on a second apprentice for about twelve thousand a year after the grant and arranges to share apprentices with two other pig farmers. Teaches Callum the data side slowly.
S1.feel: Calm, with a strong sense of responsibility for the young.
S1.quote: A government scheme teaches you to fill in forms about pigs. A farmer teaches you to see a sow is about to farrow by the way she's nesting.
S1.fieldNote: He combines a traditional view of who should train young people with an eager use of technology. He's relaxed about Callum leaving, seeing training as a duty rather than an investment. Shared apprentices is a practical, community-minded idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort it out in time, and the government shouldn't panic. New jobs will come, they always do. People should be ready to retrain and move, and stop waiting to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's closer to home than I'd say in public. Kirsten's job at the dental surgery is bookings and billing, and that's exactly the routine stuff. And our second son, Nils, works in logistics planning for a supermarket chain, sitting at a screen all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kirsten she can stop work whenever she wants, we'd manage, and I'd mean it, even though we'd feel it. I'd ring Nils and ask what he'd do, and offer him the farm office role, doing our feed buying and pig sales, which I do badly at night. I'd still build the shed, but maybe delay it six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than I'd show. It's my family in the line of fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in public the market will sort it out. But in private you're worried. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. In the long run I believe the market will sort it out. But the long run isn't much use to Nils if he's out of work next spring. I don't want handouts for him, I want him working. If that means the farm, so be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kirsten say if you told her she could stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh at me. She likes her job, she likes the people. She'd say, Adam, I'm not sitting at home watching you stare at pig dashboards. She'd find something else, probably helping at the church or the school. She's never been idle a day in her life.

S2.say: I'd say the market will sort it out in time and the government shouldn't panic. People should be ready to retrain and move instead of waiting to be rescued.
S2.think: Privately it's close to home, because Kirsten does bookings and billing at the dental surgery and our son Nils plans logistics at a screen for a supermarket.
S2.do: Tells Kirsten she can stop work whenever she likes and offers Nils the farm office job handling feed buying and pig sales. Still builds the new shed, but delays it six months.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more than he'd show, because his family is in the line of fire.
S2.quote: In the long run I believe the market will sort it out. But the long run isn't much use to Nils if he's out of work next spring.
S2.fieldNote: He answers the gap between his public and private views head on, without backing off either. His solution, like other traditional farmers, is to bring family into the farm. Kirsten's imagined reply adds humour and shows a strong marriage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who made fortunes should invest it back into the country, build things, hire people, not sit on it. I'm not for taxing everyone to death. But I'd say the crisis needs sorting, and soon, before it turns ugly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, for the pigs, it's fine. Physical work is safe, people still eat bacon. But land prices booming makes it harder for Erik to buy more land, and harder for young farmers to get started. And if half of town loses their jobs, they'll buy cheaper pork from abroad, and our price drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lock in a two-year contract with the processor, even at a slightly lower price, so we know where we stand. I'd buy the field next door now, before prices go mad, if the bank would lend, maybe another two hundred thousand. And I'd bring Nils onto the farm properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm still in control, but it's a lot of debt in an unsettled time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Another two hundred thousand on top of the shed loan. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a big risk. Kirsten would say it's madness. But land only gets dearer, and in this picture it gets dearer fast. If I don't buy now, Erik never will. I'd sit down with the bank manager, a woman called Helen Obi who's known us twenty years, and see what she thinks. If she says no, I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people would buy cheaper pork from abroad. Would you want rules against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me would. I'm for free trade, but not free trade with people who don't keep pigs to our standards. That's not fair competition. So, yes, I'd want our standards on imports. Call it what you like.

S3.say: I'd say people who made fortunes should invest back into the country by building and hiring. I'm not for taxing everyone to death, but the crisis needs sorting before it turns ugly.
S3.think: Privately the pigs are fine, but booming land prices make it harder for Erik to buy land. Laid-off townspeople buying cheaper imported pork would drop our price.
S3.do: Locks in a two-year processor contract at a slightly lower price and seeks about two hundred thousand to buy the neighbouring field before prices rise. Brings Nils onto the farm properly.
S3.feel: Anxious but still in control, carrying a lot of debt in unsettled times.
S3.quote: I'm for free trade, but not free trade with people who don't keep pigs to our standards.
S3.fieldNote: He takes the biggest financial bet of the group, borrowing more in a boom to secure land for his son. He admits a limit to his free market views on imports. Trust in a named bank manager shows his preference for people over systems when the stakes are high.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so farmers should get ready rather than complain. I'd also say we need to make sure young people still learn real skills, because robots break and somebody has to know what a healthy pig looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be one of the first to buy. Robots that clean pens, feed, move pigs and spot illness would cut my labour costs by half. The trouble is Marek and the stockmen, and Callum. I'd be saving money by taking work off men who've been loyal to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a pen-cleaning robot and a feed robot in the first year, maybe a hundred and fifty thousand with finance. I'd make Marek the man in charge of them, with the company's training. I'd keep Callum, because I promised him a trade, and I'd move one stockman to Erik's arable side instead of letting him go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and torn. Excited about the machines, worried about the men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep Callum because you promised him a trade. What does that trade look like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe it's half pigs and half robots. But I'll buy the robot. What I won't do is raise a village of young men who've never mucked out a shed. If they never learn the animals, who fixes it when the machine's wrong?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the money work, with the loans you already have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just. If the pig price holds, the robots pay for themselves in four years. If it drops, I'm in trouble, with the shed loan and the land loan and the robots. Erik and I would have to sit down and decide what to sell. That's the honest answer. It's a lot of eggs in one basket for a pig farmer.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots are coming whether we like it or not, so farmers should get ready rather than complain. Young people must still learn real skills, because robots break.
S4.think: Privately I'd be one of the first to buy, because robots could halve my labour costs. The trouble is that I'd be saving money by taking work off loyal men like Marek and Callum.
S4.do: Buys a pen-cleaning robot and a feed robot for about a hundred and fifty thousand on finance and puts Marek in charge of them. Keeps Callum and moves one stockman to Erik's arable side instead of letting him go.
S4.feel: Anxious and torn, excited by the machines but worried about the men.
S4.quote: But I'll buy the robot. What I won't do is raise a village of young men who've never mucked out a shed.
S4.fieldNote: He embraces the robots without hesitation but sets a firm moral line about keeping young people in the trade. His debts would stack up across three pictures, and he's honest that a falling pig price could break him. Marek and Callum are the people he keeps coming back to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots. Not because I can't handle the machines, but because I'd be carrying a lot of debt while laying off men who trusted me. What would help is a stable pig price, our standards on imports, and proper apprenticeship funding so farms can keep training young people alongside the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. People forget that pigs feel things. A robot might clean a pen, but a good stockman knows when a sow is frightened. I'd want any robot rules to think about the animals, not just the jobs.

headlineQuote: But I'll buy the robot. What I won't do is raise a village of young men who've never mucked out a shed.
portrait: Adam Larsen is fifty-eight and runs six hundred sows and three hundred hectares of feed grain at Thornbury with his son Erik, his long-time stockman Marek and his apprentice Callum. He uses AI every day, is comfortable with debt, and holds traditional free market views tempered by a strong sense of duty to family and young workers. Office automation hits his wife Kirsten and son Nils, and he would bring Nils onto the farm. In the fast pictures he borrows heavily for land and robots, while holding firm that young people must still learn the animals.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries him most, because he'd be carrying heavy debt while laying off stockmen who trusted him.
whatWouldHelp: A stable pig price, the same welfare standards applied to imports, and proper apprenticeship funding so farms can keep training young people alongside machines.
